name: Bagh print (hand block printing of Bagh, Madhya Pradesh)

gi.application_no: 98 (product, 2008); 505 (logo, filed 2015-01-08, GI Journal No. 75, Certificate No. 239 dated 2016-03-31)

summary: Bagh print is a hand block printing tradition of Bagh town in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, practised mainly by the Khatri (chhipa) community, and registered as a Geographical Indication. Its signature is geometric and floral repeat patterns printed in red and black on a white ground with mordants (alum for red, iron for black) that develop colour when the cloth is boiled with alizarin and dhavda flowers in a copper vat (bhatti). The process depends heavily on flowing river water for repeated washing.

concepts.title: Bagh print
concepts.summary: Bagh prints are recognised by geometric repetitive patterns, mainly red and black block printed on a predominantly white base, using natural (vegetable) colours.
concepts.body_md:
Bagh prints are recognised by geometric repetitive patterns, mainly red and black block printed on a predominantly white base, using natural (vegetable) colours. [S1, S10]

The craft is named after the small tribal town of Bagh in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh. [S1, S10]

The craft is locally called Thappa Chappai (thappa = blocks, chappai = printing) and has been called alizarin print after the dye giving the red. [S4, S6]

The traditional printers of Bagh belong to the Khatri community (Khatri biradari), the chhipas or printers. [S1, S7]

Products include cotton bedcovers, saris (cotton, silk, chiffon), cushion and table covers, dupattas, stoles, durries and dress material. [S1]

claims.text: Bagh prints are recognised by geometric repetitive patterns, mainly red and black block printed on a predominantly white base, using natural (vegetable) colours.
claims.quote: geometric repetitive patterns in different variations and colors that are mainly red and black block printed predominantly on white base

concepts.title: Bagh town and the Baghini river
concepts.summary: Bagh is located at about 22°22'N 74°46'E with an average elevation of about 240 m; the main production centre is Bagh and the Kukshi area of Dhar district.
concepts.body_md:
Bagh is located at about 22°22'N 74°46'E with an average elevation of about 240 m; the main production centre is Bagh and the Kukshi area of Dhar district. [S1]

Bagh lies in Kukshi tehsil of Dhar district near the river Baghni, a tributary of the Narmada. [S7, S3]

The Baghini, a small rivulet, passes through the town. [S5, S4]

Bagh is known for the Bagh caves, Buddhist rock-cut caves with mural paintings. [S8, S4, S3]

concepts.title: Khatri migration from Larkana, Sindh
concepts.summary: The Khatri community of chhipas is believed to have come to Bagh about 400 years ago from Larkana in Sindh, famous for its Ajrak prints.
concepts.body_md:
The Khatri community of chhipas is believed to have come to Bagh about 400 years ago from Larkana in Sindh, famous for its Ajrak prints. [S1, S8]

What motivated the families to leave Sindh is not known for sure, but they carried a strong tradition of hand block printing. [S1]

The Khatris moved from Larkana to Gujarat and Rajasthan about four centuries ago and later settled in Manawar, Madhya Pradesh. [S6]

An artisan family states that its link with block printing goes back to the seventh century AD. [S8]

concepts.title: Ismail Khatri family route: Sindh, Pali, Gautampur, Manawar, Bagh (1962)
concepts.summary: Ismail Khatri said his ancestors moved out of Sind, settled in Pali (near Jodhpur), moved to Gautampur in Malwa after a famine, and then to Manawar in Nimar.
concepts.body_md:
Ismail Khatri said his ancestors moved out of Sind, settled in Pali (near Jodhpur), moved to Gautampur in Malwa after a famine, and then to Manawar in Nimar. [S1, S3]

The community believes its ancestors first settled together in the Marwar region; many Khatris converted to Islam under the influence of a sufi saint. [S1]

Ismail Khatri's father settled in Bagh in 1962 after persuasion from local mahajans. [S3]

The Khatris settled in Bagh in 1962 via Pali, the Marwar Thar and Manawar. [S4]

Ismail Suleimanji Khatri settled in Bagh in 1962. [S6]

concepts.title: Alternative origin accounts (Jawad / Rajasthan; ~1000 years)
concepts.summary: Bagh hand block printing is believed to be about one thousand years old, passed down within families; the exact date of origin is difficult to point out.
concepts.body_md:
Bagh hand block printing is believed to be about one thousand years old, passed down within families; the exact date of origin is difficult to point out. [S1]

Some claim the craft migrated from Jawad in Mandsaur district of Madhya Pradesh or from Rajasthan. [S1]

Other former printing centres in Madhya Pradesh include Ashta, Sehore, Narsinghpur, Khairola and Javad, most now largely extinct. [S3]

concepts.title: Prints for specific communities and Adivasi wear
concepts.summary: Artisans formerly made different prints and even different clothes for different communities and castes (e.g. Brahmin, Khatri, Harijan, Bhil, Bhilala, Jat, Bharur, Mahajan); now only Adivasis retain this, for particular occasions.
concepts.body_md:
Artisans formerly made different prints and even different clothes for different communities and castes (e.g. Brahmin, Khatri, Harijan, Bhil, Bhilala, Jat, Bharur, Mahajan); now only Adivasis retain this, for particular occasions. [S1]

Members of different castes traditionally wore distinct block-printed attire that identified them on sight, sustaining the craft in Bagh. [S8]

The prints were originally the adornment of tribal inhabitants of surrounding villages. [S7]

Janjuri, juardana and beel are traditional Adivasi sari designs, usually in red or black. [S3]

concepts.title: Publicly honoured master artisans
concepts.summary: Ismail Khatri is described as an eminent printer and national awardee.
concepts.body_md:
Ismail Khatri is described as an eminent printer and national awardee. [S1]

Ismail Suleimanji Khatri received a national award in 1984 for a work with 1,230 geometric patterns; the Khatris are credited with training and inspiring over a thousand villagers to take up the craft. [S6]

Mohammad Yusuf Khatri of Dhar received the Shilp Guru Award for 2017 for conservation of the legacy of Bagh print. [S11]

Ismail Khatri played an important role in reviving block printing among the local Adivasi community. [S4]

concepts.title: Base fabric (cotton, silk and others)
concepts.summary: The main raw material is fabric, most commonly cotton; silk-cotton, kosa silk, chiffon, crepe, georgette and mulberry silk are also printed.

A silk cloth generally takes almost double the time of a cotton cloth of the same size. [S1, S3]

Fabrics are sourced from markets such as Indore, Mumbai, Maheshwar and Chanderi. [S1, S4]

concepts.title: Sanchara (rock salt)
concepts.summary: 3 kg of sanchara (rock salt) is dissolved in 15 litres of water as one component of the mengni solution.
concepts.body_md:
3 kg of sanchara (rock salt) is dissolved in 15 litres of water as one component of the mengni solution. [S1]

Softening uses Sanchora (a natural salt) with goat faeces and oil, soaked at least 12 hours. [S7]

Cloth is soaked in raw salt, hot water and goat dung, giving a slight yellow tint. [S5]

concepts.title: Mengni (goat dung)
concepts.summary: 10 kg of mengni is soaked in 10–15 litres of water and ground into a paste with a brick on a stone surface.
concepts.body_md:
10 kg of mengni is soaked in 10–15 litres of water and ground into a paste with a brick on a stone surface. [S1, S3]

The pre-treatment solution includes castor oil and goat droppings, trampled to produce froth. [S4]

concepts.summary: 1 kg of arandi ka tel (unrefined castor oil) is mixed with sanchara and mengni to make the dhaul solution; the oil is stirred with salt until it curdles.

1 kg of arandi ka tel (unrefined castor oil) is mixed with sanchara and mengni to make the dhaul solution; the oil is stirred with salt until it curdles. [S1, S3]

concepts.title: Harara / harda (Terminalia chebula)
concepts.summary: Treating the cloth with harara gives an off-white or off-yellow ground and strengthens the tones of the black and red printed later.
concepts.body_md:
Treating the cloth with harara gives an off-white or off-yellow ground and strengthens the tones of the black and red printed later. [S1, S3]

Bahera is not used as the alternative because it gives a blackish tinge to the fabric. [S1]

The yellowish tinge from harda is essential for the brightness of the black and red alizarin colours. [S7]

Harra is Terminalia chebula. [S5, S6]

concepts.title: Fitkari (alum) — red mordant
concepts.summary: Alum is colourless; it produces red when boiled with alizarine and dhavda flowers.
concepts.body_md:
Alum is colourless; it produces red when boiled with alizarine and dhavda flowers. [S1]

Red printing paste uses about 80–100 g of alum per litre of water. [S1]

Boiling tamarind seeds and alum first yields a fuchsia pink, which alizarin turns red. [S5, S6]

Alum is varied to produce different shades of red. [S1]

concepts.summary: Black is prepared from ferrous sulphate mixed with tamarind seed powder and glue, cooked in water and stored.
concepts.body_md:
Black is prepared from ferrous sulphate mixed with tamarind seed powder and glue, cooked in water and stored. [S1]

For black paste, hirakasish (iron sulphate) or iron filings are put in an earthen pot with jaggery and water and left for 15–20 days. [S1]

Hirakayisha was earlier made of iron rust and is now bought from the market. [S1]

Black paste is made by boiling iron rust to a thick consistency. [S4]

Black uses iron sulphate or rusted iron boiled with jaggery, lime, wheat flour and water. [S6]

concepts.title: Secondary dyes: pomegranate rind, dhavdi leaves, indigo, turmeric
concepts.summary: The four basic natural colours used extensively are red, black, khaki and indigo.
concepts.body_md:
The four basic natural colours used extensively are red, black, khaki and indigo. [S1, S3]

Mustard: pomegranate skins boiled 10–12 hours and strained; the fabric is dipped, dried on stones, three times. [S1]

Khaki: dhavdi leaves soaked and boiled 10–12 hours and strained. [S1]

Indigo was prepared from indigo leaves, lime and sajji in an earthen pot in a pit for 3 days; now indigo powder is dissolved with caustic and hydro. [S1]

Harda, bahera and anar chilka are the most common natural dyes used in Bagh units. [S7]

concepts.title: Wooden printing blocks (bilal)
concepts.summary: Blocks are intricately and deeply carved by block-makers in Pethapur in Gujarat; they are also sourced from Gandhinagar and Jaipur.
concepts.body_md:
Blocks are intricately and deeply carved by block-makers in Pethapur in Gujarat; they are also sourced from Gandhinagar and Jaipur. [S1]

Some surviving blocks are nearly 200 years old and still used. [S1]

Blocks are made of teak (sagwan) for density and water/warp resistance, drilled with a kamthi bow and saarardi bit, chiselled, and soaked in oil for several days. [S4]

Blocks (bilal) are the central tool; block wood includes sagavan and shisham. [S3]

Blocks from Pethapur have small holes that prevent staining and smudging. [S5]

concepts.title: 1. Khara karna (desizing in the river)
concepts.summary: The cloth is washed in the river, soaked about 2 hours, beaten on riverside stones, and later beaten on a stone slab to remove starch.
concepts.body_md:
The cloth is washed in the river, soaked about 2 hours, beaten on riverside stones, and later beaten on a stone slab to remove starch. [S1, S3]

Desizing removes manufacturing gums so the cloth regains its dimension and printed motifs do not get disfigured in later washing. [S7]

concepts.title: 2. Mengni karna (salt–goat dung–castor oil bath)
concepts.summary: Cloth is kept overnight in a dhaul solution of sanchara, mengni and castor oil, washed in flowing river water and dried; the process is repeated three times.
concepts.body_md:
Cloth is kept overnight in a dhaul solution of sanchara, mengni and castor oil, washed in flowing river water and dried; the process is repeated three times. [S1, S3]

The fabric is pressed hard by several men with their feet for about half an hour until it softens. [S1]

The fabric is soaked in a mixture of castor oil, goat dung (or droppings), salt and water; Gaatha describes trampling it to produce froth. [S6, S4]

Alum or hirakayisha is first made into a paint-like solution with tamarind seed; hot water adjusts density. [S1]

Alum or iron sulphate is boiled and aged 8–10 days, then thickened with chiyan powder. [S3]

concepts.title: 5. Block printing
concepts.summary: Paste is transferred from the tray to the block's raised parts and printed block after block with care and precision; an expert prints about 5 metres in two to three hours.
concepts.body_md:
Paste is transferred from the tray to the block's raised parts and printed block after block with care and precision; an expert prints about 5 metres in two to three hours. [S1, S3]

The block is dipped and stamped with a solid thud of the side of the palm; the outline block is printed first, then filling blocks. [S7]

A black boundary is stamped first and the printer works in rectangles from the outside inward, using old cloth or paper to avoid overlap. [S4]

concepts.title: 6. Resting / curing the print
concepts.summary: The printed material is dried, rolled into bundles and kept away for eight to fifteen days so the colour sets.

concepts.title: 7. Bichalna (river washing of excess colour)
concepts.summary: Two people hold the fabric under running water, each piece at least 20 minutes, then beat it against stones to remove residue.

Two people hold the fabric under running water, each piece at least 20 minutes, then beat it against stones to remove residue. [S1, S3]

If bichalna is not done correctly, permanent stains and smudges appear on the printed surface. [S1]

Washing in free-flowing water after printing removes harda completely, making the fabric white again before alizarin dyeing. [S7]

concepts.summary: The cloth is boiled in a solution of dhavda ka phool and alizarine; it is during this process that the colour of the prints develops.
concepts.body_md:
The cloth is boiled in a solution of dhavda ka phool and alizarine; it is during this process that the colour of the prints develops. [S1, S3]

Heat is increased throughout by adding firewood; the cloth is turned constantly with long sticks. [S1]

Alizarin and dhawdi are boiled for a few minutes, the temperature is then lowered, and the printed cloth immersed. [S7]

Bhatti-karna boils 30–40 fabrics with alizarin and dhavdi for about three hours with constant stirring. [S5]

Alizarin and dhavadi extracts are boiled in a copper container for five to six hours. [S4]

Each sari takes at least three weeks after printing, is washed at least three times and goes to the bhatti at least twice. [S1]

concepts.title: 9. Tarai (washing, sprinkling and sun-bleaching)
concepts.summary: After drying, the cloth is washed three to four times in the stream; while drying it is repeatedly moistened by spraying water by hand, which helps set the colours (tarai).
concepts.body_md:

Final drying is in the sun. [S5]
